rule: Known sites only (design decision 2): each location is already published by UNESCO, the National Park Service, or a state or tribal steward. Address-restricted records are excluded. Centres are approximate until verified on the LiDAR (centre.verified); frames are 3 km for the first build and shrink once verified. Town Creek Indian Mound (NC) was dropped on Oct 13: no 3DEP 1 m coverage.
compiled: 2026-10-12, from each steward's page (source_url) and the coordinate source named per site

sites.period: between 1 and 400 CE (UNESCO); built 2,000 to 1,600 years ago
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, 2023) (component 1689-002); National Historic Landmark (Newark Earthworks)
sites.steward: Ohio History Connection

centre.source: docs/spikes/lidar.md (measured on the 3DEP 1 m DEM; UNESCO's component point is 160 m east)

sites.form: a circular enclosure nearly 1,200 feet in diameter whose walls surround an interior ditch, with a gateway nearly 200 feet wide and Eagle Mound at the center
sites.notes: Coordinates are the component's entry in the UNESCO component table (the table renders client-side; it was read via the search index, not a direct fetch). The steward page also publishes 40.0402671, -82.4277555 (visitor info). Grounds open dawn to dusk; museum Wed-Sun. 455 Hebron Rd, Heath, OH. Interior ditch is 8-13 ft deep per steward.

sites.period: between 1 and 400 CE (UNESCO); built 2,000 to 1,600 years ago
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, 2023) (component 1689-001); National Historic Landmark (Newark Earthworks)
sites.steward: Ohio History Connection
sites.form: two geometric enclosures, a large circle and a larger octagon, connected by an avenue; the Observatory Mound covers a former gateway in the circle
sites.notes: Coordinates are the component's entry in the UNESCO component table (the table renders client-side; it was read via the search index, not a direct fetch). (Search snippet truncated the seconds of longitude at '45.'; 45.82 matches the Wikipedia transcription of the same table.) Steward page also publishes 40.0519828, -82.4463745. Leased to Moundbuilders Country Club as a golf course from 1910; Ohio History Connection bought out the lease and opened it for full public access on Jan 1, 2025 (https://www.ohiohistory.org/octagonsettlement). Now open during daylight hours; 125 N. 33rd St, Newark. Golf-course grading may still show in LiDAR.

sites.period: between 1 and 400 CE (UNESCO); built 2,000 to 1,600 years ago; steward: built around 2,000 years ago
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, 2023) (component 1689-008); National Historic Landmark
sites.steward: Ohio History Connection
sites.form: a hilltop enclosure of earthen embankments on a steep bluff over the Little Miami River, broken by more than 67 gateways; the largest hilltop enclosure in North America
sites.notes: Coordinates are the component's entry in the UNESCO component table (the table renders client-side; it was read via the search index, not a direct fetch). Steward page also publishes 39.4067824, -84.0893218. Ohio's oldest state park. Open Wed-Sat 10-5, Sun noon-5; admission charged. Wooded bluff, so LiDAR bare-earth is the main way to see the walls.

sites.period: between 1 and 400 CE (UNESCO); built 2,000 to 1,600 years ago; steward: used as a ceremonial center for approximately 400 years
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, 2023) (component 1689-006); unit of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park
sites.steward: National Park Service (Hopewell Culture National Historical Park)
sites.form: a Great Enclosure in the general shape of a parallelogram; remnants of the eastern, western and northern walls remain visible
sites.notes: Coordinates are the component's entry in the UNESCO component table (the table renders client-side; it was read via the search index, not a direct fetch). Steward page also publishes 39.3608166, -83.0844809. Type site of the Hopewell culture. Walls plow-reduced and nearly invisible on the ground; good LiDAR/magnetometry story. Grounds open dawn to dusk. NPS prohibits drones at all park units.

sites.period: between A.D. 1-400 (NPS)
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, 2023) (component 1689-004); unit of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park (proclaimed Mound City Group National Monument, 1923)
sites.steward: National Park Service (Hopewell Culture National Historical Park)
sites.form: 25 mounds inside a low earthen wall forming a slightly irregular square with rounded corners, with gateways in the east and west sides
sites.notes: Coordinates are the component's entry in the UNESCO component table (the table renders client-side; it was read via the search index, not a direct fetch). hopewellearthworks.org publishes 39.3744923, -83.0065767. All visible mounds and walls are modern restorations on intact bases (only fully restored Hopewell complex). Visitor center daily 9-4; grounds dawn to dusk. 16062 State Route 104, Chillicothe.

sites.period: between 1 and 400 CE (UNESCO); built 2,000 to 1,600 years ago
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, 2023) (component 1689-005); unit of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park
sites.steward: National Park Service (Hopewell Culture National Historical Park)
sites.form: a circle joined to an octagon, the same geometry as Newark's Octagon Earthworks, where Paint Creek meets the Scioto River
sites.notes: UNESCO publishes the component's location (N39 17 54.82 W82 55 6.56, read via the search index). An NPS research preserve, open to the public only by special arrangement: kept under decision 2 (location published by UNESCO), shown from LiDAR only. Form and dimensions to confirm on the LRM (task 1.3).

sites.period: between 1 and 400 CE (UNESCO); built 2,000 to 1,600 years ago
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, 2023) (component 1689-003); National Historic Landmark (1964); unit of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park
sites.steward: National Park Service (Hopewell Culture National Historical Park)
sites.form: an irregular square with rounded corners and a slightly overlapping circle of nearly equal area, with smaller circles and parallel walls running toward the Scioto River
sites.notes: Coordinates are the component's entry in the UNESCO component table (the table renders client-side; it was read via the search index, not a direct fetch). hopewellearthworks.org publishes 39.3790743, -82.9809185. Reopened Aug 2016; open daylight hours with a 1.1 mi round-trip trail to an overlook. Walls are plow-leveled; NPS itself produced a 2012 LiDAR elevation map, so this is a strong LiDAR demo.

sites.period: Between 1 - 400 A.D. (NPS)
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, 2023) (component 1689-007); unit of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park
sites.steward: National Park Service (Hopewell Culture National Historical Park)
sites.form: a tripartite enclosure: a large partial circle, a smaller circle attached on the west and a precise square attached on the southeast, with the reconstructed Central Mound inside the great circle
sites.notes: Coordinates are the component's entry in the UNESCO component table (the table renders client-side; it was read via the search index, not a direct fetch). hopewellearthworks.org publishes 39.2416867, -83.2214086. Most walls are no longer visible; only the Central Mound is fully restored. Grounds open dawn to dusk. 7058 US 50 East, Bainbridge.

sites.culture: disputed: Ohio History Connection favors a Late Precontact builder (around AD 1100); other archaeologists argue Early Woodland (around 300 BC)
sites.period: around AD 1100 (Ohio History Connection's view) or around 300 BC (alternative view)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark
sites.steward: Ohio History Connection
sites.form: an effigy mound in the shape of a serpent, laid out in a crescent-like plan on a narrow bluff above the confluence of East Creek and Ohio Brush Creek
sites.notes: COORDINATES FROM WIKIPEDIA INFOBOX (fallback); steward page publishes none. ohiohistory.org returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so steward content was read via search-index snippets; it loads in a browser. Open 10-5 with a museum; base width 6-7.6 m. Dating debate source: https://ohiohistory.org/ohios-serpent-mound-an-american-indian-story-written-in-the-earth. The Shawnee Tribe co-hosts solstice events here (https://shawnee-nsn.gov/news/summer-solstice-2024/).

sites.period: Adena culture (800 B.C. to A.D. 100), built in several stages (Ohio History Connection)
sites.designation: National Register of Historic Places
sites.steward: City of Miamisburg (city park); listed as an Ohio History Connection site
sites.form: a conical burial mound, one of the two largest conical mounds in eastern North America, on a 100-foot ridge above the Great Miami River
sites.notes: COORDINATES FROM WIKIPEDIA INFOBOX (fallback). City park at 900 Mound Ave; concrete steps lead to the top. Ohio History Connection locator page (bot-blocked, read via search index) gives the dimensions and dating and says the mound holds 54,000 cubic yards of earth.

sites.period: an estimated 2,000 years ago (steward)
sites.designation: National Register of Historic Places
sites.steward: Arc of Appalachia, managing on behalf of the Ohio History Connection
sites.form: a stone-and-earthen-walled hilltop enclosure following the rim of a flat-topped ridge, bordered on the inside by a substantial ditch, with a second small circular earthwork on the south side of the preserve
sites.notes: COORDINATES FROM WIKIPEDIA INFOBOX (fallback); likely the preserve, not the enclosure itself. Wall 6-15 ft high with about 36 openings per Arc (Ohio History Connection says 33 gateways). Reached only by hiking; heavily forested, so LiDAR bare-earth is ideal.

sites.period: Mississippian period (800-1350 at this site) (UNESCO); occupied from 700 to 1400 (Illinois DNR)
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (1982); National Historic Landmark; Illinois State Historic Site
sites.steward: Illinois Department of Natural Resources
sites.form: a city of platform, ridgetop and conical mounds dominated by Monks Mound, a terraced platform mound and the largest prehistoric earthen mound in the Americas, plus a reconstructed stockade and Woodhenge
sites.notes: Coordinates are the UNESCO property point (198bis), read via the search index. Grounds open daily dawn to dusk (https://cahokiamounds.org/); stairs to the top of Monks Mound. Preserves 70-72 of about 120 original mounds; some mounds sit on unprotected land outside the site.

sites.culture: Effigy Moundbuilders (Late Woodland); probably ancestors of the Ho-Chunk and other Midwestern tribes (NPS)
sites.period: effigy mounds date to about AD 650-1200 (NPS)
sites.designation: National Monument (1949)
sites.steward: National Park Service
sites.form: more than 200 mounds on bluffs above the Mississippi River, 31 of them bird- and bear-shaped effigies, including the 10-bear Marching Bear Group
sites.notes: COORDINATES FROM WIKIPEDIA INFOBOX (fallback); likely near the visitor center, and the mound groups spread over separate north and south units (Fire Point Trail has Little Bear and Great Bear; Marching Bear is a 4-mile guided hike). The NPS itself cites LiDAR as revealing mound extent. 20 culturally associated tribes consider the mounds sacred. Dimensions read from an NPS PDF via search snippet.

sites.culture: Middle Mississippian (living alongside local Woodland people)
sites.period: thrived between A.D. 1000 and 1300 (DNR); fortified town established 1050-1100, abandoned about 1200 A.D. (DNR history)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark
sites.steward: Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources
sites.form: large flat-topped pyramidal (platform) mounds inside a log-and-clay stockade; two mounds and portions of the stockade have been reconstructed
sites.notes: Coordinates read from the DNR park page HTML (map point). Open 6 a.m.-11 p.m. year-round; vehicle sticker required. Three platform mounds originally; two survive restored.

sites.period: established by A.D. 1100; abandoned by 1450 (Indiana State Museum)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark
sites.steward: Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites
sites.form: 11 earthen platform mounds built to elevate important buildings, on the Ohio River near Evansville, with a recreated palisade
sites.notes: Coordinates are the map-marker point on the steward's plan-your-visit page (probably the interpretive center); Wikipedia's infobox (37.9425, -87.4572) is about 0.7 km south-west. Dimensions are from Indiana's state tourism site, not the museum page. 600-acre site; self-guided outdoor tours 10-4:30. Sacred place to today's tribal nations.

sites.period: Great Mound believed constructed around 160 B.C.; Early Woodland tradition, over 2,000 years old (Indiana DNR)
sites.designation: National Register of Historic Places
sites.steward: Indiana Department of Natural Resources, Division of State Parks
sites.form: the largest of 10 earthworks, an earthwork with an outer embankment at the center of a ceremonial complex aligned to solstice sunsets over neighboring mounds
sites.notes: Coordinates are waypoint 2 ('Great Mound') of the DNR's GPS History Adventure brochure. The steward pages give no dimensions, so none are listed. 4306 Mounds Rd, Anderson, IN.

sites.culture: Late Archaic (Poverty Point culture); built by hunter-fisher-gatherers
sites.period: constructed 3,700-3,100 years ago (UNESCO); between 1700 and 1100 B.C.E. (NPS)
sites.designation: UNESCO World Heritage (2014); National Monument; National Historic Landmark; Louisiana State Historic Site
sites.steward: Louisiana Office of State Parks (State of Louisiana)
sites.form: six concentric semi-elliptical (C-shaped) earthen ridges around a plaza, with large mounds including Mound A, possibly a bird effigy
sites.notes: Coordinates are the UNESCO property point (read via search index); the Louisiana Division of Archaeology page gives GPS 32.63622, -91.405026 for the site marker. lastateparks.com blocks automated fetches. One of the six mounds is privately owned and not accessible. 2.6-mile self-guided hike; museum and tram tours.

sites.period: occupied from around A.D. 1000 until A.D. 1450 (steward)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark
sites.steward: The University of Alabama Museums
sites.form: 29 flat-topped earthen platform mounds arranged around a vast central plaza on a bluff over the Black Warrior River, once enclosed on three sides by a bastioned palisade
sites.notes: COORDINATES FROM WIKIPEDIA INFOBOX (fallback). The steward pages give no mound heights (the often-cited 58 ft for Mound B is from non-steward sources, so it is omitted). Park preserves 326 acres (https://moundville.museums.ua.edu/about/). The ancient-site page says 26 mounds within the enclosure; the about page says 29. ua.edu returned HTTP 405 to one fetcher but loads normally.

names: Etowah Indian Mounds State Historic Site
sites.period: 1000 A.D. to 1550 A.D. (steward)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark; Georgia State Historic Site
sites.steward: Georgia Department of Natural Resources, State Parks & Historic Sites
sites.form: six earthen mounds with a plaza, village site, borrow pits and defensive ditch; the tallest is a platform mound likely used for the priest-chief's home
sites.notes: Coordinates are the 'GPS Coordinates' the steward page publishes (likely the visitor center/address, 813 Indian Mounds Rd SE, Cartersville). Steward calls it the most intact Mississippian site in the Southeast.

sites.culture: Mississippian (one of four precontact cultures at the park)
sites.period: mounds created by Mississippians in the 10th century CE (NPS); Earth Lodge floor carbon-dated to 1015 CE
sites.designation: National Historical Park
sites.steward: National Park Service
sites.form: flat-topped pyramidal platform mounds (the Great and Lesser Temple Mounds) raised in stages, with a reconstructed earth lodge and other mounds
sites.notes: Coordinates are the NPS place record for the Great Temple Mound Complex (NPS places API, which backs that page's map). Park has 7 mounds and 8 miles of trails; steps to the top of both temple mounds. Ancestral homeland of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation.

names: Plum Bayou Mounds Archeological State Park
Toltec Mounds Archeological State Park (former name)
sites.period: late-Woodland through early-Mississippian Period, inhabited from A.D. 650 to 1050 (Arkansas State Parks)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark; Arkansas State Park
sites.steward: Arkansas State Parks (Arkansas Archeological Survey research station on site)
sites.form: a ceremonial complex of earthen mounds beside an oxbow lake, enclosed on its other three sides by a ditch and earthen embankment
sites.notes: Renamed from Toltec Mounds. Coordinates read from the map data embedded in the steward page (Wikipedia's 34.6469, -92.0653 is about 0.5 km west). Dating read via search snippet of https://www.arkansasstateparks.com/articles/archeology-plum-bayou-mounds (blocks automated fetch). Visitor center Wed-Sat 8-5, Sun 1-5.

sites.period: construction from about 250-150 B.C. (steward)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark
sites.steward: West Virginia Department of Arts, Culture & History
sites.form: a conical burial mound, one of the largest Adena mounds, originally encircled by a ditch crossed by at least one causeway
sites.notes: COORDINATES FROM WIKIPEDIA INFOBOX (fallback). In downtown Moundsville; the surrounding ditch was about 40 ft wide and 5 ft deep per the steward. Museum and research center on site.

sites.period: Middle Woodland Period (200 B.C. to 500 A.D.) (Tennessee State Parks)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark
sites.steward: Tennessee State Parks
sites.form: at least 17 mounds, including Sauls Mound, one of the tallest Middle Woodland mounds in the United States
sites.notes: Coordinates read from the steward park page (probably the museum); Wikipedia's 35.4978, -88.6825 is about 0.6 km east. Stairs to an observation deck on Sauls Mound. The state archaeology program calls it the largest mound complex in Tennessee.

sites.period: built and used between 1200 C.E. and 1600 C.E. (NPS)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark (1989); Natchez Trace Parkway, milepost 10.3
sites.steward: National Park Service (Natchez Trace Parkway)
sites.form: a large flat-topped platform mound with two secondary mounds on top; the second-largest Mississippian Period ceremonial mound in the United States
sites.notes: Coordinates are the NPS place record (NPS places API). Covers eight acres; total height about 60 ft with the secondary mounds. NPS removed the summit stairs in 2017 at associated tribes' request (https://www.nps.gov/natr/learn/news/natchez-trace-parkway-removes-stairs-from-emerald-mound.htm); visit the grounds, do not climb.

sites.culture: Mississippian (MDAH: likely ancestral to the Natchez people)
sites.period: people thrived in this area from about AD 1000 to 1450 (MDAH)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark
sites.steward: Mississippi Department of Archives and History
sites.form: platform mounds and two large plazas, dominated by Mound A, the Temple Mound
sites.notes: COORDINATES FROM WIKIPEDIA INFOBOX (fallback). 12 of the original 23 mounds survive. MDAH asks visitors not to walk on the mounds. The MDAH Mound Trail page dates the Mississippian occupation ca. AD 1200-1600.

sites.period: occupied by Native Americans from 350 to 900 C.E. (steward)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark; Georgia State Park
sites.steward: Georgia Department of Natural Resources, State Parks & Historic Sites
sites.form: a platform mound (Mound A) dominating two smaller burial mounds and several ceremonial mounds
sites.notes: CHECK BEFORE LIDAR: the steward's 'GPS Coordinates' point is about 1.8 km west of Wikipedia's infobox point (31.471467, -84.929367) and is probably the park office/entrance, not the mound group. Steward calls Mound A the largest Woodland-period platform mound in Eastern North America.

sites.period: between approximately AD 850 and 1450 (Oklahoma Historical Society)
sites.designation: National Register of Historic Places
sites.steward: Oklahoma Historical Society
sites.form: a mound center of original earthworks along the Arkansas River, including Craig Mound, the site's only burial mound
sites.notes: Added candidate. Coordinates are embedded in the steward's visit page. Craig Mound was badly looted in the 1930s and reconstructed in the 1970s on its original location, so LiDAR shows the reconstruction. The only prehistoric American Indian archaeological site in Oklahoma open to the public.

sites.culture: Mississippian (NPS documentation calls Mound A a Late Mississippian temple mound)
sites.period: about 800 years ago; inhabitants left around A.D. 1200 or 1300 (NPS)
sites.designation: National Historic Landmark (1989); within Shiloh National Military Park
sites.steward: National Park Service (Shiloh National Military Park)
sites.form: seven earthen mounds inside a former palisade on a Tennessee River bluff between two ravines: six rectangular flat-topped platform mounds and one oval, round-topped burial mound
sites.notes: Added candidate. Coordinates are the NPS place record for tour stop 3, 'The Center of Town' (NPS places API); the orientation shelter is at 35.14141, -88.32684. No steward mound dimensions found. 1.1-mile trail; park open daily.
